readerTitle: Why Walmart's winning formula lost in Germany
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Walmart 독일 진출과 철수, 1997~2006; 비교 사례 Walmart de México) + 가상 적용 (사무실 청소 회사)
insight: 해외로 가져갈 수 있는 것은 방법이지 우위 자체가 아니다. 본국의 규모·공급망·고객 적합성처럼 장소에 묶인 우위는 새 시장에서 처음부터 다시 만들어야 한다.
misconception: Walmart는 인사하고 웃는 문화를 강요해서 독일에서 실패했다. 본국에서 통한 방식이면 해외에서도 통한다.

sources.text: Knorr, A. & Arndt, A. (2003). Why did Wal-Mart fail in Germany? Universität Bremen, Materialien des Wissenschaftsschwerpunktes Globalisierung der Weltwirtschaft, Bd. 24.
Walmart press release (July 2006) on the sale of its German stores to Metro; contemporary coverage, e.g. The New York Times and BBC News, July 2006
Bundeskartellamt decision (2000) on below-cost grocery sales by Wal-Mart, Aldi and Lidl; upheld by the Federal Court of Justice (2002)
Coverage of the Wuppertal labor court ruling on Walmart's German ethics code (2005)
Rugman, A. & Verbeke, A. on location-bound vs non-location-bound firm-specific advantages, e.g. Rugman, A. (2005). The Regional Multinationals. Cambridge University Press.
Walmart annual reports and Walmart de México history (Cifra acquisition, 1990s); Walmart South Korea exit (2006) press coverage

factChecks.note: 인수 시점: 1997년 Wertkauf(약 21개 매장), 1998년 Interspar(약 74개 매장). 합계 약 95개로 적었습니다. 게시 전 Walmart 자료와 Knorr & Arndt(2003)로 확인하세요.
2006년 Metro에 매각한 매장 수(약 85개)와 손실 규모(약 10억 달러로 널리 보도)는 2006년 7월 보도자료와 언론 보도로 확인하세요. 카드에는 "widely reported at about $1 billion"으로만 적었습니다.
분데스카르텔암트의 원가 이하 판매 금지 결정(2000년)의 대상 품목(우유, 버터, 설탕, 밀가루 등)과 대상 기업(Wal-Mart, Aldi, Lidl)을 확인하세요. 카드에는 "certain groceries"로만 적었습니다.
영어를 경영 언어로 썼다는 내용은 여러 사례 연구에 나오지만 세부가 다릅니다. 카드에는 "reportedly"로 표시했습니다.
Wuppertal 노동법원(2005)이 윤리강령 일부(사내 연애 관련 조항 등)를 무효로 본 판결 내용을 확인하세요.
독일의 대형 매장 입지 규제(도시계획 규정)와 영업시간법(Ladenschlussgesetz)이 진출 당시 적용되었는지 확인하세요.
Walmart de México가 미국 밖 최대 사업 중 하나라는 서술과 Cifra 지배 지분 인수 시점(1997년)을 연차보고서로 확인하세요. 한국 철수(2006년, 신세계 이마트에 매각)도 확인하세요.

cards.title: Why Walmart's winning formula lost in Germany
body: In 1997, the world's largest retailer entered Germany by buying two local chains.
In 2006, it sold its German stores to rival Metro and left, with a loss widely reported at about $1 billion. The usual story blames forced smiles. The real lesson runs deeper.

image.label: A big-box store with its shadow shrinking on the pavement
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 거대한 대형마트 건물이 작은 독일풍 거리 위에 놓여 있고, 바닥에 비친 그림자는 건물보다 훨씬 작게 줄어든 모습. 실제 Walmart·Metro 로고, 색상 배지, 상표 사용 금지.

cards.title: It's 1998. You just bought about 95 German stores.
body: Many of the stores are older. Your rivals include Aldi and Lidl, discount chains with very low prices and thousands of stores across Germany.
At home, your edge is low prices built on enormous scale. What's your plan?

options.text: Roll out the home playbook fast: same low-price model, same service style, leaders from headquarters
options.feedback: Speed and consistency feel safe. But this assumes your home advantages came with you, and that shoppers, staff and rules work as they do at home.

options.text: First find where you can actually beat Aldi and Lidl in Germany, then decide what to keep and what to change
options.feedback: Slower and less satisfying. But it tests which of your strengths really travel before you spend money betting on them.

options.text: Cut prices hard to win share now, and fix the stores later
options.feedback: Price matters a lot to German shoppers, so the instinct is fair. But without home-level scale, each price cut hurts you more than it hurts a local discounter.

choice.afterReveal: Walmart largely chose a mix of A and C.

cards.title: The home model, shipped as is.
body: Walmart brought much of its US approach. Staff were asked to greet shoppers and bag groceries, which many Germans found odd or unwanted. Early leaders came from the US, and English was reportedly used in management.

It also cut prices hard. In 2000, Germany's competition authority ruled that Walmart, Aldi and Lidl must stop selling certain groceries below cost. Unions clashed with management, and a German court later struck down parts of its staff ethics code. Losses ran for years.

cards.title: Location-bound advantages
body: Some strengths go anywhere: know-how, systems, a brand. Others are tied to a place. Researchers call these **location-bound advantages**.

Walmart's low prices rested on thousands of US stores, its own distribution network and huge buying power with American suppliers. None of that crossed the Atlantic. In Germany, with fewer than 100 stores, Walmart was a small chain facing discounters that were giants on their home ground.

image.label: A suitcase holding 'methods' while 'scale' and 'suppliers' stay behind
image.brief: 플랫 일러스트. 대서양을 건너는 여행 가방 안에는 "Methods", "Systems" 카드가 들어 있고, 출발 항구에는 "Scale", "Supplier power", "Distribution network" 상자가 남겨져 있음. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Four places the advantage leaked away.
body: Studies of the case point to gaps on four fronts:
list: **Customers:** German shoppers already had very low prices from discounters
**Rivals:** Aldi and Lidl were local champions with the scale Walmart lacked
**Rules:** limits on opening hours, on below-cost selling and on building large stores
**People:** US-style service and management clashed with German workplace norms and strong unions
cards.callout: The smile story is the one people remember. The scale gap was the one that cost money.

cards.title: Where buying abroad worked better.
body: In Mexico, Walmart bought control of Cifra in the 1990s, a retailer that was already a market leader. It gained local scale, local suppliers and local know-how from day one. Walmart de México grew into one of the company's largest businesses outside the US.
The point isn't "never buy abroad." It's that what you buy must give you the position your advantage needs.
cards.softwareNote: A product built on network effects starts with no network in a new country. The code travels. The crowd of users that made it valuable does not.

cards.title: Don't turn one case into a rule.
body: Walmart also left South Korea in 2006, but it has done well in other markets. Hindsight makes every failure look obvious, and plenty of smart people backed the German move at the time.

Culture stories are also easy to tell and can hide the economics. A business can adapt its greeting style perfectly and still fail, because it never reaches the scale or position its model depends on.

image.label: A world map with some markets marked green and others grey
image.brief: 단순한 세계 지도 인포그래픽. 몇몇 국가는 초록색 체크, 독일과 한국은 회색 "Exited 2006" 표시. 실제 기업 로고 없이 중립적인 아이콘만 사용.

cards.title: Now it's office cleaning.
body: Your company cleans offices. At home you hold hundreds of contracts in one city, so crews drive short routes between sites and you underbid every rival.
A big client asks you to clean its offices in another country, where you'd start with just a few sites. How do you price?

options.text: Match your home prices. Your system is your edge
options.feedback: Your methods travel, but route density doesn't. With a few scattered sites, crews spend paid hours driving, and the low price turns into a loss.

options.text: Price for the costs you'll really have, and build density in one city before competing on price
options.feedback: You may lose some bids early. But you only compete on price once you've rebuilt the advantage that made low prices possible.

options.text: Partner with a local cleaning firm that already has dense routes
options.feedback: This borrows the local position you lack, which is smart. The cost is shared margin, less control, and depending on someone else's quality.

cards.title: Before you go abroad, ask which advantages stay home.
body: Walmart's methods crossed the ocean. Its scale, supplier power and fit with local customers did not.
**Try it today:** list three reasons customers choose you over rivals. For each, ask: would this still be true in a new city or country where I start from zero?
